title: Vapor of vapors
sum: A narrator introduces "Qohelet, son of David, king in Jerusalem" and sums up his teaching in one cry: "Vapor of vapors... Everything is vapor" (1:1–2). Then comes the question the book will test: "What gain is there for a person in all his toil that he toils under the sun?" (1:3). A poem answers it with the world itself. Generations pass, the earth stays, the sun pants back to its place, the wind turns, the streams run to a sea that never fills, and the eye and ear are never satisfied. "Nothing at all is new under the sun" (1:9), and nothing is remembered (1:11).

At 1:12 Qohelet begins to speak for himself, as a king over Israel in Jerusalem. He set his mind to explore everything that is done, and found it "vapor and chasing the wind" (1:14). Wisdom showed him what could not be straightened or counted, and the more he knew, the more it hurt (1:15–18).
readings: The opening says at once that nothing lasts and nothing is gained. The poem's circles are pointless, and the king's wisdom only multiplies pain. On this reading the chapter sets the tone for a book that strips away every comfort, including the comfort of wisdom itself (Crenshaw; Fox's 'absurd').
Read as a teacher's clearing of the ground

Others read the chapter as a sober prologue, not a final verdict. The world is stable and ordered (1:4), and human attempts to master it fail because people are creatures, not because the world is meaningless. The book will go on to name the gifts that are real: food, drink, work and love from God's hand (2:24). The opening clears away false hopes so that these can be seen (Whybray; Bartholomew).

views.H: Qohelet's question about 'gain' is a businessman's question, and many scholars hear the commercial life of Persian or early Greek Judea behind it: coins, trade, profit and loss (Seow). The royal voice of 1:12 recalls Solomon, Israel's model of wealth and wisdom (1 Kings 3–10), but the book is set in a world where Judea had no king of its own.
views.C: The book's outer voice speaks of Qohelet in the third person (1:1–2; 7:27; 12:8–14). Most critics see a frame narrator, either the author or a later editor, who introduces and finally judges Qohelet's words. The late Hebrew of these verses, with words such as 'inyan, 'task' (1:13), known otherwise from Aramaic and the Mishnah, points to the Persian period or later.
views.W: The royal autobiography of 1:12–2:26 has the shape of ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions and of Akkadian 'fictional autobiographies', in which a famous king tells his deeds and draws a lesson (Longman). The cycle of nature has parallels in Greek thought, but Qohelet does not borrow its ideas of eternal recurrence; he uses the cycles as images of human weariness.
views.J: The rabbis debated this book's place in Scripture because its words seemed to contradict one another and to lean toward heresy (Bavli Shabbat 30b; Leviticus Rabbah 28:1), yet they kept it, reading its opening with its ending in mind. The Targum tells that Solomon was driven from his throne for his pride and wandered weeping, 'I, Qohelet, was king' (1:12). The book is read in synagogues at the Feast of Booths.
views.X: Christian readers from Gregory of Nyssa and Jerome onward read 'Vapor of vapors' as a call to look beyond the passing world to God. The Imitation of Christ quotes it in its first chapter: all is vanity except to love God and serve him alone. Paul's 'subject to emptiness' (Romans 8:20) uses the Greek word for hevel, and many read Ecclesiastes 1 as a picture of the creation waiting for its freedom.

deep.b: For Ecclesiastes 1–4 the Hebrew text is the Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008), read through the site's word-by-word Hebrew and its machine list of the codex's Ketiv and Qere readings (there is one in these chapters, at 4:8). The Greek was checked verse by verse in Rahlfs' critical edition (the CCAT text) and in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus. 'The Greek' on these pages means Rahlfs' text; where Vaticanus differs, it is named. The Dead Sea Scrolls were checked in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook: 4QQoh-b (4Q110), from the first century BC, has visible letters from 1:8–16, best preserved in 1:10–14. Where its letters are visible it agrees with the Leningrad Codex except in spelling (it writes extra vowel letters, as in kol and lo'), in one small grammatical change ('asher na'asu for shenna'asu, 'that are done', in 1:14), and in reading 'in Jerusalem' with the Greek at 1:16 (see the variant). The Syriac Peshitta, the Targum and Jerome's Latin are cited as reported by the commentaries named in each note (chiefly Seow, Fox and Knobel's translation of the Targum); Jerome's Latin readings at 2:8, 3:11 and 3:21 are well known and given as he translated them.

The book never says 'Solomon'. It says 'son of David, king in Jerusalem' (1:1), and in 1:12–2:26 the speaker describes a life that only Solomon lived: unmatched wisdom, great building, gold, singers and many women (1 Kings 3:12; 1 Kings 10; 1 Kings 11:3). For most of Jewish and Christian history this settled the question. The Talmud says Hezekiah's scribes wrote the book down (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), and rabbinic tradition said Solomon wrote it in old age, after the Song of Songs and Proverbs.

Three things led most modern scholars, including many conservative ones, to another view. The Hebrew is late, close to the Hebrew of the Mishnah, with Aramaic words and two Persian loanwords (pardes, 2:5; pitgam, 8:11). After chapter 2 the speaker views kings from below, as an official or subject (4:13–16; 8:2–4; 10:16–20). And the name Solomon, which a writer claiming his authority would surely use, is absent. On this view a sage of the Persian or Greek period took on Solomon's role for two chapters, as a thought experiment: if anyone could find lasting gain, it would be Solomon. Luther already doubted that Solomon wrote it himself (Table Talk), and Franz Delitzsch, a conservative Lutheran, wrote in 1875 that if the book were Solomon's there would be no history of the Hebrew language. Some evangelical scholars still defend Solomonic authorship, pointing to the book's own words and to the possibility that its language reflects a northern dialect or a later updating (Gleason Archer; Walter Kaiser).

Two voices speak in the book. Qohelet says 'I'. Another voice, heard in 1:1–2, in the small aside 'says Qohelet' (7:27) and in the epilogue (12:8–14), speaks about him. Michael Fox calls this voice the frame narrator: he presents Qohelet as a wise teacher, quotes him and finally gives his own judgment, that people should fear God and keep his commands (12:13). Some think the frame narrator is the book's real author, who created Qohelet as a character; others that he is an editor or disciple who gathered his teacher's words; others that two or more editors added the epilogue (see 12:9–14). The frame matters for how one reads the whole: the book does not simply say 'everything is vapor'; it reports that Qohelet said so, and invites the reader to weigh it.

echoes: 1 Kings 3:12; 1 Kings 4:29–34; 1 Kings 10:14–29; Psalm 19:5–6; Psalm 104; Isaiah 43:19; Revelation 21:5; Romans 8:20; Psalm 39:5; Proverbs 27:20

settings.what: Title, motto and the poem of the circles
settings.by: The frame narrator, who presents Qohelet's words (the poem of 1:4–11 may be Qohelet's own)
settings.to: Readers of the finished book: students of the wise and thoughtful Judeans who knew the teaching of Proverbs
settings.when: at the opening of the book, before Qohelet speaks in his own voice
settings.why: To give the verdict first ('everything is vapor') and the question that will be tested ('what gain?'), and to show in the poem that nature itself moves without arriving. Knowing that a narrator speaks here means readers hear Qohelet's words as a report to be weighed, not as the book's last word.
settings.readers: For Jews at the Feast of Booths, when the book is read, the opening sets a sober tone at the happiest feast of the year: the harvest is a gift, not a possession. For Christian monks, from Jerome onward, it was a call to despise the passing world.
views: Traditional readers hear Solomon himself, looking back on his life, perhaps after turning away from God (1 Kings 11), and writing so that others need not repeat his mistakes.
Many scholars place the book among educated Judeans of the 400s–300s BC, when coins, trade, land grants and royal taxes were new facts of life (Seow).
A teacher in the early Greek period
Others think of Judea under the Ptolemies of Egypt in the 200s BC, a time of tax farmers and of new Greek questions about happiness and fate (Hengel; Fox; Krüger).

settings.by: Qohelet, speaking as a king over Israel in Jerusalem
settings.to: Students of the wise in a scribal setting, and the educated Judeans of the Persian or early Greek period who read the finished book, all trained in the confident teaching of Proverbs (Proverbs 3:13–18)
settings.when: as Qohelet looks back on his search
settings.why: To show that the most gifted searcher, a king with every resource, found that wisdom brings pain and cannot fix what is bent. For hearers taught that wisdom could master life, this is the first blow. Knowing that the voice is royal explains the scale of the claims: if a king found no lasting gain, no one will.
settings.readers: Readers who took the speaker as Solomon heard the warning of a wise man who had seen everything; readers who take him as a later teacher hear a thought experiment in Solomon's role.
views: The king is Solomon, telling what he learned (traditional Jewish and Christian readers).
A later teacher uses the form of a royal autobiography, as ancient writers did, to test what wealth and wisdom give (most modern scholars; Longman).

title: The king's experiment
sum: Qohelet tests joy. He keeps wisdom in charge while he tries wine, builds houses, plants vineyards and parks with every fruit tree, digs pools, acquires slaves and herds, gathers silver, gold, singers and many women, and denies himself nothing (2:1–10). His heart took joy in it all, and that joy was his share. But when he looked at what his hands had done, "everything was vapor and chasing the wind. There was no gain under the sun" (2:11).

He turns to wisdom and folly. Wisdom is better, as light is better than darkness, but one fate meets the wise and the fool, and both are forgotten (2:12–16). So he hates life and his toil, which he must leave to an heir who may be a fool (2:17–23). Then the chapter turns: "There is nothing good for a person but to eat and drink and let himself see good in his toil", and this comes "from God's hand" (2:24–26).
readings: Read as a story of failure

The king tries every path to lasting satisfaction and every one fails. Pleasure fades, works pass to others, wisdom dies with the fool. The conclusion in 2:24 is resignation: since nothing lasts, take what pleasure you can (Crenshaw).
Read as a story of gift

The king fails because he tried to gain joy by his own effort. When he stops grasping, he finds that joy is a gift: the same eating, drinking and work, received from God's hand, are good (2:24–26). This is the first of the book's seven calls to joy (Whybray; Bartholomew; Luther).

views.H: The king's projects match what 1 Kings tells of Solomon (1 Kings 7; 9–11), but the words for parks (pardes, a Persian loan) and provinces (medinot) belong to the Persian empire, whose kings and nobles built walled parks and drew tribute from provinces. A wealthy Judean of that age would recognize the list as the life of the very rich.
views.C: Scholars debate whether 2:26, which seems to say God rewards the good and frustrates the sinner, is Qohelet's own view, a quotation he rejects ('this too is vapor'), or a pious editor's addition. Most now read it as Qohelet's: God gives as he pleases, and even that is beyond human control. The Greek differs in several small places (2:3, 2:12, 2:15, 2:25; see the variants).
views.W: Royal boasts of building, gardens and wealth fill ancient Near Eastern inscriptions. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, the ale-wife Siduri tells the grieving king to fill his belly, celebrate day and night, wear clean clothes and take joy in his wife and child, for that is the lot of humans (Old Babylonian version, the Sippar tablet); Qohelet's call to joy in 2:24 and 9:7–9 is often compared with it (see 9:7–10). Egyptian harpers' songs urged diners to 'make holiday' because no one returns from death.
views.J: Rabbinic readers took the king's luxury as Solomon's, and some saw his many women as the beginning of his fall (1 Kings 11:1–8). The Targum and the midrash turn the eating and drinking toward the joy of Torah and good deeds. The repeated advice to find joy fits the Feast of Booths, at which Israel was commanded to rejoice (Deuteronomy 16:14–15).
views.X: Jerome read the passage both literally and spiritually, the food and drink of 2:24 pointing to Christ's body and blood. Medieval monks used the king's failure as a warning against the world. Luther, against them, said the book does not condemn the things God made but the human heart that is never content; it teaches us to use present gifts with thanks and leave the future to God.

deep.h: The king's list and the garden of Eden
deep.b: The list in 2:4–8 recalls Genesis 2. God 'planted' a garden in Eden, made every tree that is good for food grow there, and sent a river to water it (Genesis 2:8–10). Qohelet 'planted' vineyards and parks, put every kind of fruit tree in them and made pools to water them. Several of the same verbs and nouns appear (plant, garden, every tree, water), though not in the same order. Some scholars think the echo is deliberate: the king tries to build his own paradise and finds that it gives no lasting gain (Verheij). The theme returns at 3:20, where all return to the dust, as Adam was told (Genesis 3:19). Qohelet's experiment is, on this reading, a replay of the human story: the attempt to have everything, ending in death.

Ecclesiastes repeats its advice to enjoy life seven times: 2:24–26; 3:12–13; 3:22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10; and 11:7–12:1. Each time it grows stronger, from 'there is nothing good but...' to the direct commands to go and eat one's bread with joy (9:7) and to rejoice in one's youth (11:9). R. N. Whybray argued in 1982 that these passages are the book's message: Qohelet is a 'preacher of joy' who commends the good things God gives in a world where lasting gain is impossible. Others reply that the joy is a consolation inside a dark picture, not a cure for it (Crenshaw; Fox). The phrase 'from God's hand' (2:24) is the key on either reading. Joy cannot be earned or stored; it can only be received.

echoes: 1 Kings 7:1–12; 1 Kings 9:15–19; 1 Kings 10:14–29; 1 Kings 11:1–8; Genesis 2:8–10; Psalm 49:10; Isaiah 22:13; 1 Corinthians 15:32; Luke 12:16–21; Deuteronomy 16:14–15; Matthew 6:34

settings.what: The test of pleasure and great works
settings.by: Qohelet, in the role of the king
settings.to: The educated, propertied Judeans of the Persian or early Greek period who first read the book, some of whom could afford a share of such pleasures
settings.when: as the king reports the experiment of his reign
settings.why: To show from the inside that having everything does not give lasting gain, against the hope that wealth, pleasure and great projects can make life secure. Because the speaker is a king with unlimited means, no reader can say the test was not done fairly.
settings.readers: Wealthy Judeans of the Persian or Greek period, who could afford some of these pleasures, heard a warning against seeking security in them. Christian monks heard a reason to leave them altogether.
views: Traditional readers hear Solomon himself, looking back on his life, perhaps after turning away from God (1 Kings 11), and writing so that others need not repeat his mistakes.
A later teacher writes in Solomon's role, using what 1 Kings tells of him (most modern scholars).

settings.what: Wisdom, death, the heir and the gift of joy
settings.by: Qohelet, still speaking as the king
settings.to: Students of the wise, who were taught that wisdom leads to life (Proverbs 3:13–18)
settings.why: To show the limit of wisdom: it is better than folly, but it cannot stop death or control the heir. Then to point to what remains: eating, drinking and seeing good in one's work, received from God's hand. Knowing that the hearers were trained in wisdom explains why Qohelet takes such care to say wisdom is better before saying it cannot save.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book heard the first of seven calls to joy. At the Feast of Booths it fits the command to rejoice; Luther and the Reformers heard in it the goodness of ordinary work.
views: Joy is a consolation in a world without gain (Crenshaw).
Joy is God's real gift once the search for gain is given up (Whybray; Bartholomew).

title: A time for everything
sum: "Everything has its season" (3:1). A poem of fourteen pairs names the times of life, from giving birth and dying to war and peace (3:2–8). Then Qohelet reflects. People cannot gain by their toil, because the times are set (3:9–10). "Everything he has made beautiful in its time", and God has "put forever in their hearts", yet no one can find out his work from beginning to end (3:11). So the good that remains is to be glad, to eat and drink and see good in one's toil as God's gift, and to fear the God whose work stands forever (3:12–15).

Qohelet then looks at injustice: wickedness sits in the courts (3:16). God will judge, for every deed has its time (3:17). But humans die like animals. They share one breath and go to one place, from dust to dust, and "Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above...?" (3:18–21). So a person should be glad in what he does, since no one can see what comes after him (3:22).
readings: The poem teaches the wise to know the right moment: when to speak and when to keep quiet, when to embrace and when to keep away (Proverbs 15:23). Life is a matter of discernment.
Read as a lesson in limits

The poem and the verses after it say that the times belong to God. People cannot choose or change them, nor see the whole. The right response is reverence (3:14), gratitude for daily gifts (3:13) and humility about death (3:18–21) (Fox; Krüger).
Every time, even mourning and death, has its place in a world God has made beautiful in its time. Many readers, at funerals and in grief, have found the poem a comfort: sorrow is not the whole story.

views.H: The courts where wickedness sits (3:16) were the town gate and the offices of royal judges and governors. Under Persian and Ptolemaic rule, appointed officials held great power over farmers and traders, and redress was hard to find. Qohelet writes as one who has seen this without being able to change it.
views.C: Scholars debate whether 3:17, with its promise of judgment, is Qohelet's view or an editor's addition; most now read it as his, held in tension with what he sees (3:16, 18–21). The vowels of 3:21 in the Masoretic Text keep the question but turn 'whether it goes up' into 'which goes up', so the verse seems to assume that the human spirit rises (see the variant). The poem of 3:2–8 may be older than the book and quoted by Qohelet.
views.W: Greek thinkers spoke of kairos, the right moment, and Stoic writers urged living in agreement with the order of nature. Some scholars see a meeting with such ideas in 3:1–15, though Qohelet's God is not the Stoic world-reason. The question of 3:21 is closer to Greek debates about whether the soul rises after death.
views.J: The midrash reads the poem line by line through Israel's history and Jewish law (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 3). The rabbis read 3:15 as God taking the side of the pursued, from Abel to Israel (Leviticus Rabbah 27:5). Jewish tradition affirms the world to come and the resurrection of the dead (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1), and medieval commentators read 3:21 in harmony with 12:7.
views.X: Christians have read 3:11 as the longing for God that only eternity can fill. Paul's 'the time has been shortened' (1 Corinthians 7:29) and Jesus' "My hour is not here yet" (John 2:4) are often set beside the poem. The questions of 3:18–21 are central in Christian debates about the soul after death (see the card below).

deep.b:
The poem has fourteen pairs, twenty-eight 'times'. It begins with birth and death, the frame of every life, and ends with war and peace, the frame of every society. Between them come planting and uprooting, killing and healing, building, weeping, mourning, dancing, stones, embraces, seeking, keeping, tearing, sewing, silence, speech, love and hate. The pairs alternate between what most people welcome and what they fear, but not in a fixed order, as if to say that life does not let us arrange its seasons. Seven is the number of completeness, and two sevens make the point twice: this is all of life.

What does the poem teach? If 3:1–8 stood alone, it might be practical advice: know the right time. But Qohelet follows it at once with the question 'What gain?' (3:9) and with God's control of the times (3:10–15). So most readers take the poem as a description of the world human beings live in: a world of times they did not set and cannot change, in which the wise person accepts each time as it comes and receives the good of each day as God's gift (3:12–13).

The verse holds two truths together. 'Everything he has made beautiful in its time': each moment of the poem has its fitting place. And God has 'put forever in their hearts': people sense a whole beyond the moment, a past and future larger than their own lives. Yet they cannot 'find out the work God has done, from the beginning to the end'. Human beings are made to ask about the whole and unable to see it. That is both a dignity and a frustration, and it is why Qohelet commends trust and reverence rather than mastery (3:14). The word 'forever' is debated (see the note): some read 'the world' and some, changing the vowels, 'ignorance'. With 'forever', the verse is the book's most hopeful saying about human nature, and Christian readers since Augustine have heard in it the restless heart that rests only in God.

Qohelet begins with injustice in the courts (3:16) and affirms that God will judge (3:17). Then he looks at death. As far as anyone can see, humans and animals share 'one fate' and 'one breath': both die, both go to 'one place', both return to dust (3:19–20). He asks, 'Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above, and whether the spirit of animals goes down below to the earth?' (3:21). Later he says that 'the spirit goes back to God, who gave it' (12:7) and that 'the dead do not know a thing' (9:5; compare 9:10).

Jewish readings. The rabbis knew these verses could sound like a denial of the world to come; that is one reason some wanted the book withdrawn (Leviticus Rabbah 28:1; Bavli Shabbat 30b). They kept it, and Jewish teaching affirms the world to come and the resurrection (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). Medieval commentators such as Ibn Ezra read the Masoretic vowels of 3:21 ('the spirit which goes up') as taking the rising for granted, and took the verse with 12:7 to teach that the human spirit, unlike the animal's, rises to God. Others read Qohelet as speaking only of what can be seen.

Christian readings. Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant teaching holds that the human soul survives death and is judged, while awaiting the resurrection of the body. They read 3:19–21 as a description of death as it appears 'under the sun', or as Qohelet's honest question before the fuller revelation of the New Testament (2 Timothy 1:10), and 12:7 as the answer. Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses read the verses as teaching that a person does not have an immortal soul: at death the breath of life returns to God, the person is unconscious, and hope lies in the resurrection. Many biblical scholars, apart from church teaching, think Qohelet himself did not expect a life after death and that the book's 'who knows?' is meant seriously (Crenshaw; Fox); others think he was questioning a popular belief that the spirit rises to the heavens, without denying God's power (Seow). The card below sets out the churches' answers.

echoes: Proverbs 15:23; Deuteronomy 4:2; Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Genesis 7:22; Psalm 49:12; Psalm 104:29; Job 34:15; John 2:4; 1 Corinthians 7:29; 2 Timothy 1:10

settings.what: The poem of times and God's work
settings.by: Qohelet (the poem itself may be an older piece he quotes)
settings.to: Students of the wise, and anyone who thinks the right timing or effort can secure a gain
settings.when: after the king's experiment, as Qohelet turns from his own life to the order of the world
settings.why: To show that the times of life are set by God and cannot be controlled, so that the right response is not grasping but reverence and the grateful use of each day. Knowing that the hearers were trained to seize the right moment explains the turn in 3:9: even knowing the times gives no lasting gain.
settings.readers: At funerals and in grief, the poem has been read as comfort; at the Feast of Booths, as a reminder that harvest joy has its season; for Christian monks, as a lesson that only God's work lasts.
views: The wise act at the right moment (many older commentators).
The times are God's, not ours (Fox; Krüger).

settings.what: Injustice, judgment and the death of humans and animals
settings.to: Students of the wise and the book's first Judean readers, who had been taught that the righteous live long and the wicked are cut off (Proverbs 10:27)
settings.when: as Qohelet looks at the courts and at death
settings.why: To hold together two things he believes: God will judge, and death comes to all alike. He humbles human pride by pointing to the animals, and leaves the question of what lies beyond death open. Because his hearers took long life and good name as wisdom's reward, he presses hard on death, which takes the righteous with the wicked, and asks those who expect the righteous to be vindicated in this life to look again.
settings.readers: These verses have been read in every debate about the soul: by the rabbis, who feared they denied the world to come; by Christian teachers who read them with 12:7; and by Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses, who read them as teaching that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection.
views: No one knows what follows death (Crenshaw; Fox).
Qohelet questions those who were sure the spirit rises (Seow).
Read with the Masoretic vowels and 12:7, the human spirit goes up to God (Ibn Ezra; many traditional readers).

traditions.q: Do 3:19–21 and 12:7 mean that the human spirit lives on, conscious, after death?
views: Yes. The soul is spiritual and immortal, created directly by God; at death it is separated from the body, receives judgment and awaits the resurrection (Catechism 366, 1005, 1021–1022). Ecclesiastes describes death as it appears, and 12:7 says that 'the spirit goes back to God, who gave it'.

Yes. The soul survives death by God's grace and awaits the resurrection, and the Church prays for the departed; Old Testament texts that speak darkly of death are read in the light of Christ's resurrection.

Yes. 'The bodies of men after death return to dust... but their souls, which neither die nor sleep, having an immortal subsistence, immediately return to God who gave them' (Westminster Confession 32.1, using 12:7).

Yes, though Luther often spoke of death as a sleep: the souls of believers rest in God and are awake to him until the resurrection. Lutherans confess the resurrection of the body and life with Christ after death (Philippians 1:23).

No. A human being does not have an immortal soul; at death 'the breath of life' returns to God, and the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. 3:19–21, 9:5 and 9:10 are read as plain teaching (Fundamental Beliefs 7 and 26).

No. The soul is the person, and it dies; the spirit that returns to God is the life force, not a conscious self. The hope of the dead is the resurrection, and 9:5 shows that 'the dead know nothing at all' (New World Translation).

title: The oppressed and the lonely
sum: Qohelet looks at the world from below. He sees the tears of the oppressed, "with no one to comfort them", while power is in their oppressors' hands, and he counts the dead happier than the living and the unborn happier than both (4:1–3). He sees that much work is driven by rivalry with the neighbor. The lazy fool ruins himself, but one hand filled with rest is better than two fists full of toil (4:4–6).

He sees a man alone, with no son or brother, toiling without end and never asking whom it is for (4:7–8). "Two are better than one": they help each other up, keep each other warm and stand together, and a three-ply cord is hard to break (4:9–12). Last comes a story: a poor, wise young man rises from prison to replace a foolish old king, and the crowds follow him, but those who come later will not be glad in him (4:13–16).
readings: Qohelet sees injustice clearly and does not excuse it. His praise of the dead is the cry of one who cannot stop oppression. On this reading the chapter stands beside the prophets, though it calls for no action.

Qohelet offers what can be done under the sun: work enough, but not so much that rivalry eats your life; do not live alone; value a friend or partner. The poor wise youth shows that wisdom matters more than rank, even if fame does not last.

views.H: Oppression by those with power (4:1), rivalry in trade (4:4) and the rise and fall of kings in public favor (4:13–16) fit Judea under foreign rule. Many scholars point to Ptolemaic Judea in the 200s BC, when tax farmers such as Joseph son of Tobiah grew rich and the poor had no court to appeal to (Josephus, Antiquities 12.4); others point to the Persian period.
views.C: The chapter is a set of separate observations joined by the words 'I turned and saw' (4:1, 7) and by 'better than' sayings (4:3, 6, 9, 13). The story of 4:13–16 is so brief that scholars cannot agree who is meant or even how many young men there are. Several sayings (4:5, 4:12) may be proverbs Qohelet quotes.
views.W: The wish never to have been born (4:2–3) is found in Greek poets and in Job and Jeremiah. The three-ply cord (4:12) appears in the Sumerian poem Gilgamesh and Huwawa, where Gilgamesh urges his companion on with sayings about two together. Hesiod's 'good strife', in which neighbor competes with neighbor, is close to 4:4.
views.J: The Talmud reads the poor wise youth as the good impulse and the old foolish king as the evil impulse, which comes first in a person's life and rules the body like a king (Bavli Nedarim 32b). The verses on two and three (4:9–12) are often applied to marriage and to study with a companion.
views.X: Christian readers have applied 4:9–12 to friendship, to marriage (with God as the third strand) and to life in community; Jesus sent his disciples out two by two (Mark 6:7; Luke 10:1). The tears of the oppressed with no comforter have been read beside the promise of the Comforter (John 14:16) and of God wiping away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

deep.b: Qohelet repeats one phrase twice in 4:1: the oppressed have 'no one to comfort them'. The same words echo through Lamentations, which says five times that ruined Jerusalem has no one to comfort her (Lamentations 1:2, 9, 16, 17, 21), and Isaiah answers with God's 'Comfort, comfort my people' (Isaiah 40:1). Qohelet offers no comfort himself. He does not explain the oppression, blame the oppressed or promise a reversal. He sees it, and he says that it would be better not to exist than to see it (4:2–3). This honesty is part of why the book has been precious to readers who suffer: it refuses easy answers. It is also why some readers find it unbearable. Qohelet will later say, 'It is better to be a living dog than a dead lion' (9:4), so 4:2–3 is not his final word on life, but it is not taken back either.

echoes: Lamentations 1:2; Isaiah 40:1; Job 3:11–16; Jeremiah 20:14–18; Proverbs 6:10–11; Proverbs 15:16–17; Genesis 2:18; Genesis 41:14; Mark 6:7; John 14:16; Revelation 21:4

settings.what: The oppressed, the envious and the quiet hand
settings.to: The book's first readers, educated Judeans of some means in the Persian or early Greek period, who lived under foreign officials and competed for a living in a money economy
settings.when: as Qohelet turns from the royal story to what he sees around him
settings.why: To make the reader look at oppression without excuses, and to warn against the rivalry that drives people to overwork. The two proverbs of 4:5–6 point to a middle way between idleness and grasping. If, as most scholars think, the hearers were people with some means, that explains why the warning is against too much toil, not too little.
settings.readers: Readers under foreign rule, in Persian and Greek Judea and later, recognized the oppressors. Monks and Reformers alike read 4:6 as a call to contentment.
views: Many scholars place the book among educated Judeans of the 400s–300s BC, when coins, trade, land grants and royal taxes were new facts of life (Seow).
A teacher in the early Greek period
Others think of Judea under the Ptolemies of Egypt in the 200s BC, a time of tax farmers and of new Greek questions about happiness and fate (Hengel; Fox; Krüger).

settings.what: The lonely worker and the strength of two
settings.to: Students of the wise and the Judeans who first read the book; the pictures of the road, the cold night and the attacker suit the traders and travelers among them
settings.when: in a series of observations from life
settings.why: To show that toil without a companion or an heir is vapor, and that companionship is a real good under the sun. The warning is aimed at anyone who works alone and for no one, like the man of 4:8.
settings.readers: Later readers applied the verses to marriage, friendship and community; the three-ply cord became a favorite at weddings.
views: Partners at work and on the road
The pictures fit business partners and travelers (Fox).
Many Jewish and Christian readers apply them to husband and wife.

settings.what: The poor young man and the old king
settings.to: The book's first readers, Judeans under Persian or Ptolemaic rule, who watched distant kings and their local officials rise and fall
settings.why: To show that wisdom is better than rank, yet even the wise ruler who rises from nothing will be forgotten. The story teaches readers not to put their hope in the favor of crowds or in the next king.
settings.readers: Rabbinic readers turned it inward, to the good and evil impulses (Bavli Nedarim 32b); others saw Joseph or David; modern scholars look for a ruler of Qohelet's own day.
views: Some event in the Persian or Ptolemaic period, now unknown (many scholars).
A made-up example of how popularity fades (Fox).
